question.problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+2y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=3
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an odd, $2\pi $-periodic function. Select the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)
$$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+2=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=3.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼B\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{b}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

Applying ${y}^{′}(0)=3$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =B\sqrt{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{b}_{n} \\ B\sqrt{2} & =3-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{b}_{n} \\ B & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into ${y}_{c}=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x),$ we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{\sqrt{2}})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)
$$
